transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah… thanks for seeing me. I guess I’m here because work has gotten a little harder than I’d like to admit. I’m a construction manager, and lately whenever I have to get near a scaffold, a roof edge, or an upper platform, my head just tells me I’m about to go over.

I mean, I can see the rails are there, and I know the setup is supposed to be safe. It’s not like I don’t understand that. But my mind kind of locks onto the idea that I’m going to fall anyway. I know that probably sounds a bit ridiculous, but… that’s what’s been happening.
When you get near those high places, do you suddenly have a panic attack?

I don’t know if I’d call it a full panic attack, exactly… I don’t want to overstate it. But it does hit pretty fast. Like the second I step onto temporary stairs, or even start walking toward an open upper floor, my chest tightens up, my hands get sweaty, and my legs feel like they might just lock before I can make myself take another step.

Does that count as what you mean?
Does this fear only happen when you’re in high places?

Mostly, yes. It’s really when I’m around heights at work—like getting near a scaffold, a roof edge, or one of the upper platforms. Even when I can see the rails are there and I know it’s supposed to be safe, my head still kind of tells me I’m about to go over.

I know that doesn’t sound very rational, but that’s the situation where it happens.
Do you avoid going near high places because of this fear?

Yeah… I do, more than I probably should. I try not to make a big deal of it, but I’ve been handing off a lot of the height inspections to my foremen, and if there’s a meeting that could be done on the ground level, I’ll move it there.

If I absolutely have to go up, I usually make sure someone’s right beside me, and I kind of rush through whatever I’m there to do. I’m still scared the whole time, though. I know that’s probably not ideal.
